cma-swanevelt-landscape-with-travelers.fact: Herman van Swanevelt was a Dutch painter and etcher of the Baroque era.

cma-rosa-ruins-in-a-rocky-landscape.fact: Rosa’s wild, untamed landscapes became prototypes of the Romantic landscape.

cma-lorrain-italian-landscape.fact: Claude Lorrain brought the sun and streaming sunlight into landscape painting, where it had been rare.

cma-dughet-rocky-landscape-with-hunters.fact: Gaspard Dughet was a French painter born in Rome in 1615.

cma-michel-landscape-near-paris.fact: Georges Michel was a precursor of the Barbizon school.

cma-whittredge-landscape-with-haywain.fact: A Hudson River School painter, Whittredge was president of the National Academy of Design in 1874–75.

cma-hiroshige-yokkaichi-view-of-the-mie-.fact: The Tōkaidō linked the shōgun’s capital, Edo, to the imperial capital, Kyōto: the main artery of old Japan.

cma-hiroshige-the-whirlpools-of-awa.fact: Hiroshige is considered the last great master of the ukiyo-e tradition.

cma-hiroshige-evening-snow-at-kambara-nu.fact: This series is the best-selling set of Japanese ukiyo-e prints ever made.

cma-hiroshige-gathering-shellfish-at-low.fact: Ukiyo-e usually showed actors and beauties; Hiroshige made landscapes his subject instead.

cma-hiroshige-shimosuwa-from-sixty-nine-.fact: Hiroshige made 47 of this series’ 71 prints; Keisai Eisen made the rest.

cma-hiroshige-seki-from-the-series-the-f.fact: The Tōkaidō was so popular a subject that Hiroshige made some 30 different series on it.

cma-hiroshige-night-rain-at-the-azuma-sh.fact: Hiroshige often printed one area several times and used bokashi, a color gradation, for his subtle color.

cma-hiroshige-the-snowy-garden.fact: Hiroshige’s approach was more poetic and ambient than Hokusai’s bolder, more formal prints.

cma-hiroshige-mountain-and-river-on-the-.fact: The Kiso road is also called the Nakasendō; Hiroshige’s series on it followed his Tōkaidō views.

cma-hiroshige-evening-snow-at-asuka-hill.fact: Hiroshige’s work influenced European painting at the end of the 19th century, in the wave of Japonism.

cma-hiroshige-nagakubo-station-28-from-t.fact: The series has a print for each of the Kiso road’s 69 post stations, plus Nihonbashi.

cma-hiroshige-yahagi-bridge-at-okazaki-s.fact: The Tōkaidō was the most important of the Five Roads the shogunate built to control the country.

cma-hiroshige-kano-from-the-series-sixty.fact: The Kiso road series was published by Iseya Rihei from about 1834 to 1842.

cma-hiroshige-full-moon-over-takanawa-fr.fact: Hiroshige is best known for The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō and One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.

cma-hiroshige-snow-at-the-gion-shrine-fr.fact: For collectors, Hiroshige’s death in 1858 marked the start of a rapid decline in ukiyo-e.

cma-hiroshige-picture-of-the-tenryu-rive.fact: With this series, the landscape print became a major theme of ukiyo-e.

cma-hiroshige-picture-of-matsuchiyama-fr.fact: Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji strongly influenced Hiroshige’s choice of landscape subjects.

cma-hiroshige-picture-of-the-lake-at-hak.fact: Hiroshige’s Tōkaidō series came just after Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.

cma-hiroshige-evening-bell-at-mii-temple.fact: The Eight Views of Ōmi borrow their themes, evening bells among them, from China’s Eight Views of Xiaoxiang.

cma-hokusai-rain-below-the-mountain-from.fact: The series shows Mount Fuji from different places, in different seasons and weather.

cma-hokusai-basket-of-peonies.fact: Hokusai worked until his death at 88, making over 30,000 paintings, sketches and prints.

cma-hokusai-a-view-of-mount-fuji-and-tra.fact: Hokusai made his Mount Fuji views partly in response to a travel boom in Japan.

cma-hokusai-the-brocade-bridge-in-suo-pr.fact: Hokusai helped turn ukiyo-e from portraits of courtesans and actors into an art of landscapes, plants and animals.

cma-hokusai-the-weir-at-senju-in-musashi.fact: Hokusai made the Thirty-six Views in his seventies, at the height of his career.

cma-hokusai-an-ancient-picture-of-the-bo.fact: Hokusai’s prints influenced Van Gogh and Monet during the wave of Japonisme in late-19th-century Europe.

cma-hokusai-carp-swimming-by-water-weeds.fact: Besides woodblock prints, Hokusai worked in painting and book illustration.

cma-hokusai-lumber-yard.fact: Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views were made between about 1830 and 1832.

cma-hokusai-an-ancient-picture-of-the-ei.fact: Hokusai kept working and refining his style from childhood until his death at 88.

cma-hokusai-fuji-from-surugadai-in-yedo.fact: The Thirty-six Views has been called Hokusai’s “indisputable colour-print masterpiece.”

cma-hokusai-woman-passing-a-roadside-sho.fact: The Great Wave and Fine Wind, Clear Morning secured Hokusai’s fame in Japan and abroad.

cma-hokusai-fuji-from-the-pass-of-mishim.fact: Kajikazawa in Kai Province is considered one of the finest of the Thirty-six Views.

cma-hokusai-women-and-children-walking-a.fact: Hokusai was born around 1760 and worked as a painter and printmaker in Edo-period Japan.

cma-hokusai-fuji-from-ushibori-province-.fact: The Great Wave off Kanagawa belongs to this same series of Mount Fuji views.

met-rottmann-landscape.fact: King Ludwig I of Bavaria commissioned large landscapes exclusively from Rottmann.

met-guardi-fantastic-landscape.fact: Guardi was among the last painters of the classic Venetian school.

met-dughet-imaginary-landscape.fact: Gaspard Dughet also went by the name Gaspard Poussin.

met-gainsborough-wooded-upland-landscape.fact: Though famous for portraits, Gainsborough found more satisfaction in painting landscapes.

met-bocklin-roman-landscape.fact: Böcklin’s five versions of the Isle of the Dead inspired works by late Romantic composers.

met-koninck-wide-river-landscape.fact: Koninck split his panoramas in half, horizontally, between equal measures of earth and sky.

met-rousseau-a-river-landscape.fact: Théodore Rousseau was a painter of the Barbizon School.

met-neer-landscape-at-sunset.fact: Van der Neer specialized in small night scenes lit only by moonlight and fires.

met-bourdon-a-classical-landscape.fact: Bourdon’s masterpiece, The Crucifixion of St. Peter, was painted for Notre-Dame cathedral.

met-post-a-brazilian-landscape.fact: Frans Post was the first European artist to paint landscapes of the Americas.

met-molijn-landscape-with-a-cottage.fact: Pieter de Molijn was born in London in 1595 and worked in Haarlem.

met-seurat-landscape-at-saint-ouen.fact: Seurat devised the techniques known as chromoluminarism and pointillism.

met-koekkoek-winter-landscape-holland.fact: Koekkoek is the most famous member of the Koekkoek family of painters.

met-strij-landscape-with-cattle.fact: Van Strij painted mostly landscapes: mountains, winter scenes and marines.

met-koninck-an-extensive-wooded-landscap.fact: Koninck ran a barge line between Amsterdam and Rotterdam, so his business travelled through his own landscapes.

met-denis-mountainous-landscape-at-vicov.fact: Simon Denis was born in Antwerp and died in Naples in 1813.

met-denis-mountainous-landscape-at-tivol.fact: Simon Denis was a Flemish painter who worked mainly in Italy.

met-mauperche-classical-landscape-with-f.fact: Most of Mauperché’s landscapes are capriccios.

met-daubigny-a-river-landscape-with-stor.fact: Daubigny, of the Barbizon school, is considered an important precursor of Impressionism.

met-younger-landscape-with-thatched-cott.fact: Teniers founded the Antwerp Academy and was court painter to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm.

met-daubigny-landscape-on-a-river.fact: Daubigny was a prolific etcher and one of the main artists of the cliché-verre technique.

met-gellee-pastoral-landscape-the-roman-.fact: By the end of the 1630s, Claude was the leading landscape painter in Italy.

met-corot-landscape-with-figures-les-boh.fact: Corot’s landscapes looked back to Neo-Classicism and ahead to the plein-air painting of Impressionism.
